titulo: The two conjugations: What conjugating is

aula.objetivo: Recognise the 1st and 2nd conjugations, conjugate verbs in the present tense without mixing up the endings, and learn the most common irregular verbs.

blocos.texto: (or: the untouchable stem — memorise one verb and know six forms)

blocos.titulo: What is a verb? The "happening" test
blocos.explicacao: What is a verb? The "happening" test. Before any table, the basic question: what is a verb? A verb is the word that expresses an action, a state or an occurrence. It is what a person does, is or experiences. And there is a reliable test to recognise it, the "happening" test: "I ___ at home." → live, am, stay → verb. "He ___ Russian." → speaks, studies, learns → verb. "We ___ books." → read, buy, write → verb. The verb is the backbone of the sentence. Without a verb there is no action. Without a verb there is no complete sentence. You already know how to say "Э́то но́вый дом" (this is a new house). But you cannot yet say "I am building a new house" or "He lives in a new house". That is the subject of this lesson. And the good news? The Russian verb is much more regular than you think. Much more than the noun or the adjective. The exceptions are few, and the rules are consistent. You will see.

What is a subject pronoun? (the simple truth, no fear). Before you conjugate any verb, you need to know what it is conjugated with. That means knowing the subject pronouns. "Subject pronoun" may sound like a grammar monster, but it is the simplest thing in the world. Let me take the name apart: Pronoun = a word that replaces a noun. Instead of "John" you say "he". Instead of "Mary" you say "she". Subject = it is the doer of the action in the sentence. In English, the subject pronouns are: In Russian, they are: That is all. You have used "I, you, he, she" all your life. Russian is the same: you only have to learn the matching words. No terror, no absurd memorising. Five minutes of attention is enough. Important details: • 1. Ты vs. вы. In Russian, ты is used with friends, family, children and close people. Вы is used with strangers, older people, authorities, and always for the plural. English has only "you" for both, so you must choose. • 2. Он, она́, оно́. In Russian, everything has a gender, even objects. So "table" (стол) is masculine → он; "house" (дом) is masculine → он; "book" (кни́га) is feminine → она́; "window" (окно́) is neuter → оно́. English says "it" for all of these. This is scary at first, but you already learned in lesson 11 that gender is determined by the last letter. Now you just apply it: if the noun is masculine, use он; if feminine, она́; if neuter, оно́. • 3. Они́. A single form for all three genders in the plural. It does not matter whether it is "they" (men) or "they" (women). It is always они́.

blocos.titulo: What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read)
blocos.explicacao: What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read). Before anything else, a question nobody asks and everybody should: what does it mean to conjugate a verb? To conjugate is to change the form of the verb to match the subject of the sentence. English does this very little (I speak, he speaks); Russian does it for every person. Look: Notice that the stem speak- is always the same. Only the ending changes (here just -s in the third person). You never thought "I invented a new stem" when you wrote "speaks". You just changed the ending. That is conjugating. Russian works on exactly the same principle. You have a stem (which carries the meaning) and an ending (which carries the person). The stem never changes. The ending changes. ЧИТА- + -Ю = чита́ю (I read) ЧИТА- + -ЕШЬ = чита́ешь (you read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТ = чита́ет (he / she reads) ЧИТА- + -ЕМ = чита́ем (we read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТЕ = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) ЧИТА- + -ЮТ = чита́ют (they read) The stem ЧИТА- never changed. Only the ending. Always. The difference from English is that Russian has a different ending for every person, and that is what scares beginners. But the mechanics are simple. You have just learned to conjugate a Russian verb. That is it. The rest is practice.

blocos.explicacao: The verb "scissors": the method nobody teaches. Just as we did with the adjective (lesson 12), we will apply the scissors to the verb. Remember this: every Russian verb is a LEGO of two pieces: STEM (untouchable) + ENDING (movable). And the method is always the same: • 1. Find the infinitive (the "dictionary" form, which ends in -ТЬ, -ТИ or -ЧЬ). • 2. Cut off the infinitive ending (-ТЬ, -ТИ, -ЧЬ). You have the stem. • 3. Paste on the personal ending (-Ю, -ЕШЬ, -ЕТ, -ЕМ, -ЕТЕ, -ЮТ or -Ю, -ИШЬ, -ИТ, -ИМ, -ИТЕ, -ЯТ). Done. The verb is conjugated. See it in practice with чита́ть (to read): • 1. Infinitive: чита́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: чита́ (stem) • 3. Paste the endings: чита́ + ю = чита́ю (I read) чита́ + ешь = чита́ешь (you read) чита́ + ет = чита́ет (he reads) чита́ + ем = чита́ем (we read) чита́ + ете = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) чита́ + ют = чита́ют (they read) And with говори́ть (to speak): • 1. Infinitive: говори́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: говори́- • 3. Paste the endings: говор + ю = говорю́ (I speak) говори́ + шь = говори́шь (you speak) говори́ + т = говори́т (he speaks) говори́ + м = говори́м (we speak) говори́ + те = говори́те (you speak, plural or formal) говор + ят = говоря́т (they speak). Notice: in the verb говори́ть, the vowel -и- stays in most forms (говор-и-шь) but disappears before -ю and -ят (говор-ю, говор-ят). That is normal. Why does this help? Because the Russian verb works like LEGO: instead of memorising the table, you learn to build each form. The Russian infinitive: three endings. In Russian, the infinitive (the "dictionary" form) ends in three different ways: The good news: you do not need to worry about -ТИ and -ЧЬ now. They are a minority. The vast majority of verbs end in -ТЬ, and that is what we study in this lesson.

blocos.titulo: The two conjugations: the logic behind them
blocos.explicacao: The two conjugations: the logic behind them. Here is a point that tends to stay unclear. Let us clear it up. In Russian, verbs fall into two conjugations. And the difference between them is in the personal endings: 1st CONJUGATION: 2nd CONJUGATION: How do you decide which conjugation to use? Look at the ending of the infinitive: Verbs in -ать and -ять → almost always 1st conjugation. Verbs in -ить → almost always 2nd conjugation. Verbs in -еть → mostly 2nd (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as болеть and уметь. Examples: чита́ть (to read) → ends in -ать → 1st conjugation → чита́ю, чита́ешь, чита́ет... гуля́ть (to take a walk) → -ять → 1st conjugation → гуля́ю, гуля́ешь, гуля́ет... боле́ть (to be ill) → -еть → 1st conjugation (an exception) → боле́ю, боле́ешь, боле́ет... говори́ть (to speak) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т... люби́ть (to love) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → люблю́, лю́бишь, лю́бит... звони́ть (to phone) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → звоню́, звони́шь, звони́т... Careful: there are exceptions. Some verbs in -ать, -ять, -еть belong to the 2nd conjugation. There are only eleven, and I will list them later.

blocos.explicacao: To conjugate is to change the end of the verb to show WHO does the action: I speak, you speak, he speaks. English only changes the verb in the third person singular (speak → speaks). Russian changes it for every person. The Russian present tense has only TWO conjugations, and each has its own endings. Step by step: (1) drop the -ть from the infinitive to find the stem; (2) find out the conjugation of the verb; (3) add the six endings. 1st conjugation: -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют (after a consonant, -у and -ут). 2nd conjugation: -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят (after ж, ч, ш, щ, -у and -ат). The difference is in the vowel: е in the 1st, и in the 2nd.
blocos.comparacao: an English infinitive («to speak») tells you nothing about the endings. The Russian infinitive in -ть alone is not enough either: you must learn the conjugation together with the verb; the next session gives the practical rules.
